newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Foreign interest in Kazakh T-bills falls - dealers.
newsitem.headline: Foreign interest in Kazakh T-bills falls - dealers.

text.p: Foreign investors, once keen buyers of Kazakh Treasury bills, are less active now and may leave the market following sharply lower yields, dealers said on Wednesday.

"Foreign investors are now much less interested in buying Kazakh T-bills," said Oleg Tsurkan, chief dealer at ABN AMRO Bank Kazakhstan. "They are turning to Russian or Ukrainian papers which pay much higher yields."

The yield on Kazakh 12-month MKM discount T-bills fell to 15.74 percent annual on Monday, from 22.59 percent annual at the last auction on May 6. Three-month paper fell on Tuesday to 10.30 percent from 12.29 percent on May 27.
Yields on Russian and Ukrainian T-bills average over 20 percent annual.
In January this year Kazakh T-bills paid 26 to 35 percent annual, depending on their maturity, and aggressive buying by foreigners was largely viewed as the main reason for the nose-dive in yields.

"Indeed, at some stage foreign investors were the main reason for steeply falling yields. But not now, when many local banks are only planning to leave for other markets while foreigners have already decided so," Tsurkan said.

The government and the National Bank say falling yields reflect lower inflation -- the government expects inflation to fall to 14 percent this year, from 28.7 percent in 1996. The central bank inflation target is still 17 percent.
Mukhametzhanov said banks' returns from investment in T-bills were already too low to pay interests on deposits from private persons and companies.

But many Kazakh banks still bid aggressively at T-bill auctions. At the 12-month T-bill auction on Monday bids exceeded offer by 5.6 times. Demand for three-month paper on Tuesday was 3.2 times bigger than offer.
Analysts say government securities are a safe investment compared to loans that generally bear a huge default risk.
"This illogical buying is because Kazakhstan has no other financial instrument similar to today's T-bills," a dealer from Alfa Bank Kazakhstan said.
Prime Minister Akezhan Kazhegeldin has urged local banks to invest in the stagnant economy but bankers are reluctant.
"One can talk a lot about loans to the economy but in any case they will bring much more headache than low T-bill yields," Mukhamedzhanov said.
